batch_name: Inquisition, Church, and Alchemy: Eymerich's Directorium through Del Rio's Defense
description: Three events on the changing ecclesiastical position on alchemy's legal and theological status. From Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant, 'Alchemy and the Mendicant Orders of Late Medieval and Early Modern Europe' (Ambix, 2018), which synthesizes Neil Tarrant's research on the Church's stance toward alchemy from early Christianity through the early modern period; and from Martha Baldwin, 'Alchemy and the Society of Jesus in the Seventeenth Century: Strange Bedfellows?' (Ambix, 1993), on Martin Del Rio SJ's treatment of alchemy in his Counter-Reformation demonological compendium.

persons.name: Nicholas Eymerich
persons.bio_html: Nicholas Eymerich (Nicolau Eimeric, ca. 1316–1399), a Catalan Dominican friar, served as Inquisitor General of Aragon under Pope Gregory XI and is best known as the author of the Directorium Inquisitorum (ca. 1376), the most comprehensive medieval manual of inquisitorial procedure. Eymerich received his doctorate at Avignon, served as a professor of theology, and was appointed Inquisitor General of Aragon ca. 1357. His relentless pursuit of heresy — including his campaigns against the followers of Ramon Lull — brought him into conflict with the Aragonese crown, and he was twice exiled from Aragon: once in 1360 and again in 1393, spending extended periods in Avignon. The Directorium Inquisitorum, composed in Avignon during his first exile, became the authoritative handbook for inquisitors throughout Catholic Europe; it was rediscovered and published in Rome in 1578 by the Spanish canonist Francisco Peña (ca. 1540–1612), whose commentary expanded its scope and influence dramatically. Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant, in Ambix (2018), draw on Tarrant's research to identify the Directorium as the foundational document in the Church's conceptual shift toward treating alchemy as potentially superstitious or sorcerous. Eymerich himself did not condemn alchemy outright, but his framing of the question introduced a lasting association between alchemical practice and the demonic invocations that the Directorium targeted.

persons.name: Martin Del Rio
persons.bio_html: Martin Del Rio (Martín Antonio Del Río, 1551–1608), a Belgian Jesuit, was one of the most prolific and widely read demonologists of the Counter-Reformation. Born in Antwerp of Spanish descent, Del Rio studied law and received his doctorate before entering the Society of Jesus in 1580, having previously served as a senator of Brabant and as procurator general of the army of the Spanish Netherlands. His publication record within the Society was exceptional, including commentaries on Scripture, classical texts, and moral philosophy, but he is best remembered for his three-volume Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex (Six Books of Investigations into Magic), first published at Louvain in 1599. The work went through numerous editions throughout the seventeenth century and was widely read by confessors, inquisitors, and natural philosophers across Catholic Europe. Martha Baldwin, in Ambix (1993), identifies Del Rio as having made a more careful and accepting argument for alchemy's legitimacy than was recognized by his contemporaries: he carefully argued that alchemical transmutation was not demonic, that historical claims of successful chrysopoeia (gold-making) by Arnald of Villanova, Raymond Lull, and Bernard Trevisano were credible, and that alchemy was entirely licit for pious and wealthy men. Del Rio served as professor of sacred literature at Jesuit colleges at Rouen, Liège, Graz, and Louvain.

texts.title: Directorium Inquisitorum (Eymerich)
texts.analysis_html: The Directorium Inquisitorum (Handbook for Inquisitors), composed ca. 1376 by the Aragonese Dominican Nicholas Eymerich (ca. 1316–1399) during his first exile in Avignon, is the most comprehensive medieval manual of inquisitorial procedure and the foundational document in the Catholic Church's legal framework for responding to charges of heresy, sorcery, and diabolical magic. Although Eymerich did not condemn alchemy outright, the Directorium is identified by Neil Tarrant, in research synthesized by Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant in Ambix (2018), as the pivotal document in a conceptual shift within the Church: prior to the Directorium, few Christian authorities had associated alchemical practice with sorcery or heresy; after Eymerich's framing, the association between alchemy, demonic invocation, and occult practice began to take institutional form. Eymerich distinguished between diabolical and natural magic, and introduced a framework in which practices previously treated as mere fraud could be prosecuted as diabolical if they involved implicitly or explicitly invoking demonic aid. The Directorium was not printed until 1503 (Barcelona), but it circulated in manuscript; its decisive influence on the Church's stance toward alchemy came when the Spanish canonist Francisco Peña (ca. 1540–1612) published a heavily annotated edition at Rome in 1578, with a commentary that explicitly extended Eymerich's sorcery framework to alchemical practice and enormously expanded the work's circulation and authority among Counter-Reformation inquisitors.

texts.title: Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex (Del Rio)
texts.analysis_html: The Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex (Six Books of Investigations into Magic) by the Belgian Jesuit Martin Del Rio (1551–1608), first published at Louvain in 1599, was the most comprehensive and widely read demonological compendium of the Counter-Reformation. The work went through numerous editions throughout the seventeenth century. Martha Baldwin, in Ambix (1993), identifies Del Rio's treatment of alchemy in Book I, chapter 5 as significantly more permissive than his general reputation as a scourge of natural magic would suggest. Del Rio carefully distinguished between legitimate alchemy — which he described as 'the most outstanding child of physiology' in its medicinal and spagyric applications — and transmutatory chrysopoeia, which he neither fully endorsed nor condemned. He reviewed historical claims of successful transmutation by Arnald of Villanova, Raymond Lull, and Bernard Trevisano, and concluded that such claims were 'truthful and worthy of belief.' His argument for alchemy's legality drew on the well-established scholastic principle that 'art imitates nature' — that is, the alchemist's laboratory merely speeds up natural processes of metallic ripening that would otherwise occur over geological time. Del Rio's conclusion was provocative: while the state had the right to prohibit most citizens from undertaking alchemical experiments, '... it is obvious that this art is licit for rich men.' By this reasoning, members of the Society of Jesus — pious, educated, and personally poor through their vow of poverty but institutionally supported — were ideally placed to engage in alchemy legitimately.

events.title: Nicholas Eymerich Composes Directorium Inquisitorum at Avignon
events.description: Around 1376, during his first exile from Aragon in Avignon, the Dominican Inquisitor General Nicholas Eymerich (ca. 1316–1399) completed the Directorium Inquisitorum (Handbook for Inquisitors), the most comprehensive medieval manual of inquisitorial procedure and the foundation of the Catholic Church's legal response to heresy, sorcery, and diabolical magic. Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant, in Ambix (2018), synthesizing the research of Tarrant, identify the Directorium as the document that introduced a conceptual shift in the Church's position on alchemy: prior to Eymerich's framing, few Christian authorities had treated alchemical practice as superstitious or heretical. Eymerich himself did not condemn alchemy outright, but in developing his taxonomy of diabolical and natural magic — and in targeting the practices of those who invoked demonic assistance to achieve otherwise unachievable results — he created a framework under which alchemy's more extravagant claims (especially the transmutation of base metals into gold) could be associated with diabolical invocation. Zachary Matus's Franciscans and the Elixir of Life (2017), cited in the same Campbell et al. introduction, notes that the Franciscan Order had already prohibited alchemy in a series of statutes between 1260 and 1337, with the definitions issued between 1295 and 1318 explicitly linking alchemy to occult and sorcerous practices — indicating that concerns about alchemy's relationship to diabolical magic were developing within the mendicant orders in the same period. The Directorium Inquisitorum circulated widely in manuscript but was not printed until 1503 (Barcelona). Its decisive impact on the Church's formal stance toward alchemy came in 1578, when the Spanish canonist Francisco Peña published a heavily annotated new edition at Rome. Eymerich himself was a fierce opponent of the followers of Ramon Lull — a coincidence of some significance, since the pseudo-Lullian alchemical corpus was among the most widely read alchemical texts in late medieval and early modern Europe.
events.scholarly_grounding: Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant synthesized Tarrant's research showing that the Directorium Inquisitorum was the pivotal document in the Church's conceptual shift toward associating alchemy with sorcery, in 'Alchemy and the Mendicant Orders of Late Medieval and Early Modern Europe' in Ambix vol. 65 no. 3 (2018) pp.201-209. See also Zachary A. Matus, Franciscans and the Elixir of Life: Religion and Science in the Later Middle Ages (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2017), on Franciscan statutes against alchemy.

events.title: Francisco Peña Publishes Annotated Edition of Eymerich's Directorium at Rome
events.description: In 1578, the Spanish canonist and Roman Rota judge Francisco Peña (ca. 1540–1612) published a heavily annotated edition of Nicholas Eymerich's fourteenth-century Directorium Inquisitorum at Rome. Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant, in Ambix (2018), identify Peña's edition as playing a 'pivotal role' in reshaping the Catholic Church's institutional position toward alchemy during the later sixteenth century — more consequential, in this respect, than the Directorium itself, which had been relatively little known during the century and a half following its first printing at Barcelona (1503). Peña's commentary, drawing on the framework Eymerich had created to identify diabolical magic and distinguish it from natural operations, explicitly extended the inquisitorial framework to alchemical practice — in particular to those aspects of alchemy that appeared to promise impossible or supranatural results, such as the transmutation of base metals into gold. The 1578 edition was distributed throughout Counter-Reformation Europe and read by inquisitors, theologians, and confessors. The result was a significant tightening of ecclesiastical suspicion toward alchemy among Catholic authorities. This context helps explain the defensive postures adopted by later alchemical authors in Catholic Europe — the Venetian priest Giovanni Pantheus had already felt obliged in 1530 to rename alchemy 'Voarchadumia' to avoid prosecution; Martin Del Rio SJ, writing in 1599, would carefully argue that alchemy was licit in principle even while distancing it from demonic invocation; and the Franciscan Girolamo Trimarchi, in 1637, would defend alchemy within a strictly Aristotelian natural-philosophical framework specifically to avoid the association with diabolism that Peña's commentary had reactivated.
events.scholarly_grounding: Andrew Campbell, Lorenza Gianfrancesco, and Neil Tarrant identified Francisco Peña's 1578 annotated edition of the Directorium Inquisitorum as the pivotal document in reshaping the Church's institutional stance on alchemy during the later sixteenth century, in 'Alchemy and the Mendicant Orders of Late Medieval and Early Modern Europe' in Ambix vol. 65 no. 3 (2018) pp.201-209.

events.title: Martin Del Rio SJ Publishes Disquisitionum Magicarum at Louvain
events.description: In 1599, the Belgian Jesuit Martin Del Rio (1551–1608) published his Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex (Six Books of Investigations into Magic) at Louvain, dedicating the work to a broad Counter-Reformation audience of confessors and inquisitors seeking guidance on the demarcation between legitimate and diabolical practice. The work went through numerous editions throughout the seventeenth century and was widely read across Catholic Europe. Martha Baldwin, in Ambix (1993), identifies Del Rio's treatment of alchemy in Book I, chapter 5 as representing the institutional Counter-Reformation position on alchemy in its most carefully reasoned form. Del Rio distinguished sharply between spagyric and medicinal alchemy — which he endorsed as 'the most outstanding child of physiology' — and chrysopoeic or transmutatory alchemy, about which he was more cautious but by no means dismissive. He reviewed historical claims of successful gold-making attributed to Arnald of Villanova, Raymond Lull, and Bernard Trevisano, and — in marked contrast to the spirit of Francisco Peña's 1578 expansion of Eymerich's inquisitorial framework — concluded that such claims were 'truthful and worthy of belief.' Del Rio's central philosophical argument was that alchemical transmutation did not require demonic assistance: a human practitioner could arrive at knowledge of the transmutation process 'either with the devil as teacher or through human industry and zeal,' and only the first route was illicit. He further argued that the fear of demonic involvement was not sufficient reason to prohibit chrysopoeic alchemy outright: 'it is obvious that this art is licit for rich men.' Del Rio was aware that his colleagues in the Society of Jesus — including François Aguilon at Antwerp (1596) and later Athanasius Kircher at the Collegio Romano — were themselves engaged in alchemical experiments, and his defense of alchemy as a legitimate and potentially successful practice within carefully circumscribed conditions provided the theological justification for those activities.
events.scholarly_grounding: Martha Baldwin analyzed Martin Del Rio's treatment of alchemy in Disquisitionum Magicarum Libri Sex, finding that Del Rio carefully distinguished between licit and diabolical alchemy and defended chrysopoeic transmutation as licit in principle, in 'Alchemy and the Society of Jesus in the Seventeenth Century: Strange Bedfellows?' in Ambix vol. 40 no. 2 (1993) pp.41-64.
